lesson.title: Why First-Order Half-Life Never Changes
lesson.summary: Derives t1/2 = ln2/k from the first-order integrated rate law and shows, with numbers, why this half-life stays constant while the second-order half-life does not.
lesson.body:
Now the general idea of half-life from the previous section gets turned into an exact formula, using the first order integrated rate law, ln[A] = ln[A]0 - kt. By definition, at t = t1/2 the concentration has fallen to exactly half its starting value, so substitute [A] = [A]0/2 and solve for t1/2:

ln([A]0/2) = ln[A]0 - k t1/2
ln[A]0 - ln2 = ln[A]0 - k t1/2
-ln2 = -k t1/2
t1/2 = ln2 / k, which is approximately 0.693 / k

Look closely at that final result: [A]0 does not appear anywhere in it. The starting concentration cancelled out completely during the algebra. That cancellation is the entire point, and it is a direct consequence of first order kinetics removing the same fraction of whatever remains in each unit of time, as discussed when the integrated rate law was first introduced. Since it always takes the same fraction, it always takes the same amount of time to remove half, regardless of whether you are starting with a nearly full flask or one that is already mostly reacted.

Worked example, continuing directly from the first order integrated rate law section: with k = 0.0231 min^-1,

t1/2 = 0.693 / 0.0231 = 30.0 min

Check this against that earlier example, where [A]0 = 0.500 M. After one half-life (30 min), the concentration should be 0.250 M; after two half-lives (60 min), it should be 0.125 M. That second number matches, exactly, the 0.125 M computed directly from the integrated rate law at t = 60.0 min in the earlier worked example, two independent calculations landing on the same answer.

Now for the explicit contrast that is easy to get backwards on an exam. Reuse the second order example from two sections ago: k = 0.250 M^-1 min^-1, [A]0 = 0.400 M, giving a first half-life of t1/2 = 1/(k[A]0) = 1/(0.250 x 0.400) = 1/0.100 = 10.0 min, which matched the concentration dropping from 0.400 M to 0.200 M in 10.0 minutes. Now find the next half-life, starting from that new, lower concentration of 0.200 M: t1/2' = 1/(0.250 x 0.200) = 1/0.0500 = 20.0 min, double the first half-life. Compare the two reactions side by side. In the first order example, cutting the concentration in half, from 0.500 M to 0.250 M, left the half-life completely unchanged at 30.0 min. In the second order example, cutting the concentration in half, from 0.400 M to 0.200 M, doubled the half-life, from 10.0 min to 20.0 min. This is one of the most commonly confused facts in a kinetics unit: first order half-life is a fixed constant of the reaction, while second order half-life keeps stretching longer and longer as the reaction runs out of reactant. Memorize the constancy of first order half-life specifically, and do not assume it generalizes to every order.

This constancy is exactly why techniques like radiometric dating work at all: a first order half-life is a fixed, reliable clock that does not care how much of the original isotope happens to be left, and it is why a drug's elimination half-life can be quoted as one simple number and used to plan dosing intervals, rather than needing a different number for every possible starting dose.
